title: WebAssembly Component Model in Go Backends: Sandboxed Plugin Execution, Host ABI Design, and the Isolation Tradeoff
description: How the Wasm component model changes plugin execution in Go services: host ABI design, memory safety tradeoffs, and when sandbox overhead is worth it.
linkedin_post:
The Wasm component model is past the experimental phase. If you run a Go backend that needs extensible, sandboxed plugin execution—multi-tenant rule engines, platform/product team boundaries, third-party code—it's worth a real engineering evaluation.

Key mechanics most posts skip:

→ The canonical ABI is not free. Every string and byte-list crossing requires a guest allocator round-trip. At 50k events/sec, per-event FFI overhead is measurable. You either pre-size guest buffers, batch invocations, or invert control so the guest drives the loop.

→ Memory isolation is real. A trapping guest cannot corrupt host memory. But your host import surface is still an attack surface. A guest calling a host-exported Redis GET with an arbitrary key can enumerate your cache. WIT enforces types, not authorization. That lives in your Go host import implementation.

→ wazero (pure Go, no CGo) lets you attach capability tokens to context.Context and check them inside every host import. That's where your authorization boundary actually sits.

→ The component model earns its overhead in three scenarios: multi-tenant logic isolation, independent release cycles between platform and product teams, and untrusted third-party extension code. It doesn't earn it for tightly coupled internal logic or data-intensive hot paths where copying cost dominates.

→ Before committing: enumerate who authors plugins, crossing frequency, what host capabilities the plugin needs, toolchain maturity, and whether your runtime supports fuel metering for CPU limits.
